title: 21st Birthday Hangover Kit: What to Pack and How to Stay Safe
excerpt: What to put in a 21st birthday hangover kit, what to leave out, how to make it a gift, and the safety basics every friend should know before the first legal toast.
metaDescription: What to pack in a 21st birthday hangover kit, what to leave out, how to pace the night, and the alcohol poisoning signs every friend should know.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**What goes in a 21st birthday hangover kit:** a big refillable water bottle, a few electrolyte packets, a salty snack, something bland for breakfast, ginger chews, a phone charger, earplugs and a sleep mask, and a single-serve painkiller with a note about alcohol. That covers the real problems of the morning after: dehydration, a queasy stomach, poor sleep, and a headache. But the most useful thing you can bring to a 21st isn't in the bag. It's a plan for the night itself, and at least one friend who knows the signs of alcohol poisoning and is willing to call for help.

A 21st birthday is different from an ordinary night out. For many people it's the first time they're drinking legally in a bar, and the traditions around it (21 shots, free birthday rounds, a bar crawl with a sash) are built around drinking as much as possible in a short time. That's exactly the pattern that leads to the worst hangovers and, sometimes, to the emergency room. This guide covers what to pack, how to put a kit together as a gift, how to pace the night so the birthday person actually remembers it, and the safety basics every friend in the group should know.

> **This guide is for adults 21 and over.** A hangover kit makes a rough morning more comfortable. It doesn't make heavy drinking safe, and nothing in it treats alcohol poisoning. **Call 911 (in the US) if** someone is confused, can't be woken up, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Never leave a very drunk person alone to "sleep it off." If the birthday person takes prescription medicine, check with a pharmacist before the party about how it mixes with alcohol.

## Why a 21st Birthday Needs Its Own Kind of Hangover Kit

A general hangover kit assumes a normal night. A 21st birthday breaks that assumption in a few ways.

**The drinking is fast.** Birthday shots, "one from everyone," and drinking games pack a lot of alcohol into a short window. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink an hour for many adults, though it varies a lot from person to person. Drinking faster than that doesn't make the alcohol go anywhere. It just stacks up in your blood, and blood alcohol can keep rising for a while after the last drink, as alcohol still in the stomach is absorbed.

**Tolerance is often low.** Plenty of people turning 21 haven't had much to drink before, or have only had beer at parties. A night of straight spirits hits much harder than they expect.

**Everyone is buying.** Strangers at the bar, friends, the bartender. It's generous, but it means the birthday person loses track of how much they've had. Nobody is counting, which is the problem.

**It's often a bar crawl.** Walking between bars, standing in lines, dancing, and sweating all add to fluid loss. Late-night food is often skipped or grabbed at 2 a.m., after the damage is done.

**It's a gift.** A 21st kit doubles as a present. That's a nice idea, as long as the jokes in the bag don't crowd out the things that actually help.

## The Core 21st Birthday Hangover Kit Checklist

Everything here is cheap, easy to find, and safe for almost everyone.

### 1. A big water bottle

This is the single most useful item. Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin) that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you pee more than you drink. A full bottle on the nightstand means the birthday person can sip during the night and first thing in the morning without getting up. A one-liter bottle is a good size. Bonus points if it has a fun 21st design so it gets used again.

### 2. Electrolyte packets

Two or three single-serve packets. Electrolyte drinks help replace the sodium and potassium lost through extra urination and sweating, and many people find them easier to get down than plain water when they feel sick. Any common brand works. If you're unsure whether to use them before bed or the next morning, our guide on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) walks through the timing. A packet in water before bed is a reasonable habit.

### 3. Salty snacks and a bland breakfast

Pretzels, crackers, or a small bag of chips for late at night. Then something easy for the morning: instant oatmeal cups, a granola bar, a banana (if you're packing it fresh), or a note that says "eggs and toast are on me." Eating before and during drinking slows how fast alcohol gets into your blood, which is the most underrated hangover tip there is. In the morning, bland carbs and some protein are gentle on a sore stomach. If you want to know why eggs show up on every hangover list, see our post on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover).

### 4. Ginger chews or mints

Ginger has some evidence for easing nausea in other settings, like pregnancy and motion sickness, and it's a harmless thing to try for a queasy morning. Mints help with the "I can still taste last night" feeling.

### 5. A phone charger or small power bank

This one is about safety, not comfort. A dead phone at 1 a.m. means no rideshare, no way to find the group, and no way to call for help. A small charged power bank is one of the most practical things you can give someone going on a bar crawl.

### 6. Earplugs and a sleep mask

Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it tends to break up sleep in the second half of the night. You wake at 5 a.m., the room is bright, and you can't drift off again. Earplugs and a mask won't fix that completely, but they make it more likely the birthday person can sleep in. A lot of what people call a hangover is really exhaustion. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on.

### 7. A single-serve painkiller, with a note

If you include a pain reliever, choose single-dose packets, keep them in their original labeled packaging, and add a note. A simple version:

- **Not before bed or while drinking.** Neither common type of painkiller prevents a hangover.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol):** the liver handles both alcohol and acetaminophen, so the morning after heavy drinking isn't the time for extra doses. Many cold and flu products also contain acetaminophen, so it's easy to double up by accident. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers the details.
- **Ibuprofen, naproxen or aspirin:** easier on the liver but harder on the stomach, and alcohol already irritates the stomach lining. Take with food and water.

The safest version of this item is to skip it and just tell the birthday person where the pharmacy is.

### 8. Lip balm, tissues, and a toothbrush kit

Small comforts. Dry lips and a sore throat are common after a loud night of shouting over music. A travel toothbrush is welcome if they end up crashing at a friend's place.

## Optional Extras (and What to Know About Them)

These are nice to have, not the foundation.

- **A sports drink or coconut water** in the fridge for the morning.
- **Instant coffee or a coffee gift card.** Caffeine can help with the headache of caffeine withdrawal if they normally drink coffee, but it doesn't sober anyone up.
- **A comfy hoodie or "21" T-shirt** for the morning after. Part gift, part pajamas.
- **Hair ties, bobby pins, and blister plasters.** Bar crawls in new shoes are hard on feet.
- **A DHM supplement.** DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's often sold for hangovers. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, and there is no good evidence yet that it prevents hangovers in people. It's an optional extra that some people like, not a reason to drink more. More on this near the end.

## What to Leave Out of the Kit

Some popular joke items are fine. Others are a bad idea.

- **Mini bottles of liquor.** A kit is for the morning after. Adding more alcohol to a night that already involves a lot of it doesn't help anyone, and "hair of the dog" just postpones the hangover.
- **Energy drinks for mixing.** Caffeine can mask how drunk you feel without lowering how drunk you are, so people keep drinking past the point they normally would. Health agencies such as the CDC have warned about mixing the two.
- **Sleeping pills or antihistamine sleep aids.** These add to alcohol's sedating effect. Never give sedatives to someone who has been drinking.
- **Anything prescription.** Even if it's "just" a friend's spare pill, it doesn't belong in a gift bag.
- **Hangover "cure" claims.** Nothing cures a hangover except time. A cute card saying "this will cure you" sets the wrong expectation.

## How to Put the Kit Together as a Gift

A 21st kit is easy to make look good without spending much.

**Choose a container they'll reuse.** A drawstring bag, a small cooler bag, a lunch box, or a toiletry bag. Clear pouches let them see what's inside at a glance.

**Group by time of night.** One idea that works well: three small bags labeled "Before," "Bedtime," and "Morning."

- **Before:** a snack bar and a note that says "eat dinner first."
- **Bedtime:** water bottle, electrolyte packet, earplugs, sleep mask.
- **Morning:** breakfast item, ginger chews, coffee voucher, painkiller packet with its note.

**Add a personal card.** Something funny and kind beats a list of instructions. If you want to slip in one serious line, make it "text me when you're home."

**Budget.** A basic kit with a water bottle, electrolytes, snacks, ginger chews, earplugs, and a mask comes in around $20 to $35 depending on what you choose. A power bank or nicer water bottle pushes it toward $50. If you'd like more ideas or a version for a different occasion, our [hangover kit ideas guide](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas) and our [bachelorette hangover kit](/never-hungover/bachelorette-hangover-kit) cover other setups.

## 21st Birthday Safety: The Part That Matters Most

The kit helps the morning. This section is about getting to the morning safely. If you're a friend helping plan the night, this is the best gift you can give.

### Understand what "a drink" actually is

In the US, one standard drink has about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly 12 ounces of regular beer (about 5% alcohol), 5 ounces of wine (about 12%), or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof spirits. A typical shot is about one standard drink. Many cocktails, especially the big, sweet, "birthday special" ones, contain two or three. A Long Island iced tea can easily be more than that.

That matters because the classic 21st challenges are built on shots. Twenty-one shots is twenty-one standard drinks. For most people, that amount over a few hours is not a "big night." It's a dose that can stop someone breathing. Even half that number in a short time is well beyond what the body can clear.

### Why the 21-shots tradition is dangerous

The US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) defines binge drinking as a pattern that brings blood alcohol to 0.08% or higher, which usually happens after about four drinks for women or five for men in around two hours. Birthday-shot traditions go far beyond that. Alcohol poisoning happens when there's so much alcohol in the blood that the parts of the brain that control breathing, heart rate, and temperature start to shut down. It can happen to healthy young people on their first big night, and it has.

If the group wants a tradition, change the rules rather than the fun:

- **Make it 21 of something else.** Twenty-one photos, twenty-one dares, twenty-one stops on a scavenger hunt, or twenty-one dollars in tips at the karaoke bar.
- **Make shots optional and small.** One "first legal drink" toast is the moment people actually remember.
- **Water between every drink.** Ask the bartender for a water with every round. It's free, and it slows the pace.
- **Spread it out.** If the plan is a bar crawl, spend at least an hour at each spot and eat at one of them.

### Pace the birthday person, kindly

When everyone wants to buy a round, the birthday person ends up holding three drinks at once. A designated friend can quietly accept drinks "for later," swap some for soda, or nurse a drink alongside them. This isn't about policing. It's about making sure the person whose night it is gets to enjoy it, not spend it in a bathroom. For practical pacing tricks, our guide on [how to not get drunk](/never-hungover/how-to-not-get-drunk) has more ideas, and our [party drinking tips](/never-hungover/party-drinking-tips) cover the basics for any big night.

### Eat a real dinner first

Food in the stomach slows the rate alcohol reaches the bloodstream. A proper meal with protein, fat, and carbs before going out is one of the most effective things you can do. Plan the dinner into the night so it doesn't get skipped.

### Plan the ride home before you leave

Decide in advance: a designated driver who isn't drinking at all, a rideshare, a taxi, or a short walk home together. Make sure the birthday person's phone is charged and that at least two friends know where they're sleeping. Agree that nobody goes home alone with someone they just met, and nobody is left behind at the last bar.

### Assign a "buddy" for the night

One friend who drinks lightly or not at all and has agreed to keep an eye on the birthday person. This person knows the warning signs below, knows the address of where everyone is staying, and is willing to make the call if something looks wrong.

## When to Get Help: Alcohol Poisoning Warning Signs

This is the box to screenshot and share with the group chat before the party. According to the NIAAA, signs of alcohol poisoning include:

- **Confusion or stupor**, meaning someone is awake but not making sense, or barely responsive
- **Trouble staying conscious, or can't be woken up**
- **Vomiting**, especially while drowsy or passed out
- **Seizures**
- **Slow breathing** (fewer than eight breaths a minute) **or irregular breathing** (ten seconds or more between breaths)
- **Slow heart rate**
- **Clammy skin, very low body temperature, or bluish or pale skin**
- **Dulled responses**, such as no gag reflex

**You don't need to see all of these.** If someone has even one or two, call 911. If you're unsure, call anyway. Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) can also give advice, but for someone who is unresponsive or has trouble breathing, 911 comes first.

**While you wait for help:**

- Stay with them. Don't leave them alone for even a few minutes.
- If they're lying down, roll them onto their side (the recovery position) so they won't choke if they vomit.
- Keep them warm.
- Don't give them coffee, a cold shower, or more food or drink to "sober them up." None of these lower blood alcohol, and some make things worse.
- Don't let them "sleep it off." Blood alcohol can keep rising after they stop drinking.
- Tell the paramedics what they drank and roughly how much, and about any medicines or drugs they may have taken.

**Worried about getting in trouble?** Many US states have medical amnesty or Good Samaritan laws that offer some protection to people who call for help in an alcohol emergency, and many colleges have similar policies. The rules vary from place to place, but the basic point holds everywhere: a phone call is never the wrong choice when someone's breathing is at risk.

For a full guide, see our page on [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs). If the birthday person can't remember chunks of the night, that's a sign they drank far more than their body could handle. Our guide on [blacking out](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains why it happens.

## The Morning After: How to Use the Kit

If the night went well and the birthday person just has an ordinary hangover, here's a gentle plan for the morning.

1. **Drink water first.** Before getting up if possible. Then an electrolyte drink once the stomach settles.
2. **Eat something small and bland.** Toast, crackers, oatmeal, or a banana. Once that stays down, move to a real breakfast with some protein.
3. **Rest.** Go back to sleep if you can. Earplugs and a mask help.
4. **Go easy on painkillers.** If you take one, take a single standard dose after eating, and follow the note in the kit.
5. **Get outside, gently.** A short walk and some daylight help some people feel more human.
6. **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Drinking more only delays the hangover.

Most hangovers peak when blood alcohol drops back toward zero and get better over the course of the day. If symptoms are getting worse instead of better, or the person can't keep any fluids down, it's time to get checked out (see below).

## When a Bad Hangover Needs a Doctor

Most hangovers are miserable but harmless. A few situations need medical attention:

- **Vomiting that won't stop** or being unable to keep water down for many hours, which can lead to serious dehydration
- **Vomiting blood** or material that looks like coffee grounds
- **Severe stomach pain**, especially pain that spreads to the back
- **Confusion, extreme drowsiness, or being hard to wake** the next day
- **Chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or fainting**
- **A severe headache unlike any you've had before**, or one with a stiff neck, fever, or vision changes
- **An injury you don't remember getting**, especially a head injury

For any of these, see urgent care, call your doctor, or go to the emergency room. If someone is unresponsive or has trouble breathing, call 911.

## If You're the Birthday Person: A Short Checklist

- Eat a real dinner before you go out.
- Decide on your own limit before the first drink, and tell one friend.
- Alternate every drink with water.
- Say yes to the toast, and no to the fifth round of shots. "I'm pacing myself so I remember this" is a perfectly good answer.
- Keep your phone charged and know how you're getting home.
- Don't mix alcohol with energy drinks, sleeping pills, or anything else.
- If you take prescription medicine, ask a pharmacist ahead of time whether you should drink at all. Some antidepressants, ADHD medicines, antibiotics, and anxiety medicines don't mix well with alcohol.
- When you get home, drink a glass of water and sleep on your side.

## Where DHM Fits (Honestly)

DHM shows up in a lot of hangover kits, so it's worth being clear about what it is. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a flavonoid from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*), a plant used in traditional East Asian remedies for drinking. Lab and animal research, including a widely cited 2012 study in rats published in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, suggests DHM affects how alcohol acts on the brain, and some studies point to effects on how the liver processes alcohol. Human research is limited, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people. It doesn't lower blood alcohol enough to make heavy drinking safe, and it does nothing for alcohol poisoning.

If you want to include one as an optional extra in a 21st kit, a simple single-ingredient option is [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). People usually take it with water around the time they drink. Check with a doctor or pharmacist first if the birthday person takes prescription medicine. For more on doses, see our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025), and for the wider picture on what actually helps, read [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

The honest ranking still stands: dinner first, water between drinks, a slower pace, a charged phone, a safe ride home, and a friend who's looking out for you all matter far more than any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

A good 21st birthday hangover kit is simple: water, electrolytes, salty snacks, a bland breakfast, ginger, earplugs and a mask, a power bank, and a clearly labeled single-serve painkiller with a note about alcohol. Package it by time of night, add a kind card, and skip the mini bottles and sleeping pills.

The bigger gift is a plan for the night. Swap the 21-shots tradition for something that doesn't put the birthday person at risk, build in dinner and water, sort out the ride home, and make sure at least one friend knows the signs of alcohol poisoning and will call 911 without hesitating. That way, the birthday person wakes up a little rough, with good stories, and remembers the night.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What should I put in a 21st birthday hangover kit?**

The essentials are a large refillable water bottle, two or three electrolyte packets, salty snacks, a bland breakfast item such as oatmeal or crackers, ginger chews, earplugs and a sleep mask, a charged power bank, and a single-serve painkiller in its labeled packet with a note about alcohol. Those cover dehydration, an upset stomach, poor sleep, a headache, and getting home safely. Supplements are optional extras.

**What should I leave out of a 21st birthday kit?**

Skip mini bottles of liquor, energy drinks for mixing, sleeping pills or antihistamine sleep aids, and anything prescription. Extra alcohol and energy drinks encourage heavier drinking, and sedatives add to alcohol's effect on breathing. Also avoid cards or products that promise to cure a hangover, because nothing does except time.

**Is it safe to do 21 shots on your 21st birthday?**

No. Twenty-one shots is about twenty-one standard drinks, which for most people is far more than the body can clear in a night and is enough to cause alcohol poisoning, which can stop someone breathing. If your group wants a tradition, make it 21 of something else, such as photos or dares, and keep shots to a single toast.

**How do I keep my friend safe on their 21st birthday?**

Make sure they eat a real dinner first, get water with every round, and spread drinks out over the night. Have one friend drink lightly and act as a buddy, keep their phone charged, and agree on a safe ride home before you leave. Learn the signs of alcohol poisoning and call 911 if you see them. Never leave a very drunk person alone to sleep it off.

**What are the signs of alcohol poisoning?**

Signs include confusion, trouble staying awake or being unable to wake up, vomiting while drowsy or passed out, seizures, slow breathing (fewer than eight breaths a minute) or long gaps between breaths, a slow heart rate, and cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Someone doesn't need every sign. If you see one or two, or you're unsure, call 911, stay with them, and roll them onto their side.

**Should I give someone a painkiller before bed after drinking?**

No. Neither acetaminophen nor ibuprofen prevents a hangover, and taking them while alcohol is still in your system adds strain to the liver (acetaminophen) or stomach (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin). If a painkiller is needed, a single standard dose the next morning after eating is the more sensible choice. Anyone who takes prescription medicine should check with a pharmacist.

**Does DHM prevent a hangover on your 21st?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people. Most research on it comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It doesn't make heavy drinking safe and does nothing for alcohol poisoning. Some people include it in a kit as an optional extra, but eating, pacing, water, and a safe ride home matter far more.

**How much does a 21st birthday hangover kit cost?**

A basic kit with a water bottle, electrolyte packets, snacks, ginger chews, earplugs, and a sleep mask usually costs around $20 to $35. Adding a power bank, a nicer bottle, or a T-shirt brings it closer to $50. The most useful items are also among the cheapest.
